questions.q: What is the full extent of what a log management tool does on its own?
options: It centralizes logs and lets someone search them -- nothing more
It automatically correlates events across every source in real time
It raises security alerts without anyone asking
It matches activity against threat intelligence feeds
questions.explain: Log management's whole job is centralizing logs and enabling search -- it doesn't watch for anything or alert on its own.

questions.q: Which capability does a SIEM add on top of log management?
options: A larger storage quota, nothing else
Real-time correlation and automatic alerting across sources, plus security-specific analytics
The ability to delete logs faster
A requirement that all logs come from a single vendor
questions.explain: A SIEM adds continuous, automatic correlation, alerting without being asked, and security-specific detection logic on top of the centralized log storage log management already provides.

questions.q: In the contrast scenario from this lesson, what happens when five failed logins occur across three systems within five minutes, in an environment with only log management (no SIEM)?
options: The tool automatically raises an alert
Nothing happens until a human decides to search for it
The logins are automatically blocked
A threat intelligence feed is automatically consulted
questions.explain: Log management is passive -- without a SIEM's correlation and alerting, that pattern sits in the logs unnoticed until someone goes looking.

questions.q: According to this lesson, what is the simplest functional test for whether a tool is a SIEM or just log management?
options: Whether it can store more than one terabyte of logs
Whether it correlates events in real time and raises security alerts automatically, rather than only supporting search
Whether it has a graphical user interface
Whether it is open-source
questions.explain: The real difference is active, automatic correlation and alerting versus passive storage and search -- regardless of how good the search features are.

questions.q: Why does this distinction matter in practice, beyond terminology?
options: It doesn't matter -- the terms are interchangeable in every real-world context
It matters for accurately evaluating tools, scoping what a team actually has in place, and describing your own experience correctly in an interview
It only matters for billing purposes
It matters only to vendors, never to analysts
questions.explain: Vendors and job postings sometimes blur the line between centralized logging and a true SIEM, so knowing the functional difference matters for real evaluation and honest self-description.
